We find that water resources constrain ~30% of projected electrolytic hydrogen demand in 2030 and 2050, which is exacerbated to over 50% by stricter water usage limits. Such water constraints risk carbon mitigation opportunities of ~174–299 MtCO 2 e in 2050. We identify a city-specific cost-minimum strategy, primarily based on using reclaimed water for electrolytic hydrogen production. This strategy can unlock 99% of water-constrained mitigation opportunities, with costs only ~20% higher than using natural water in 2050.

title: Monitoring nature-based solutions is key for compliance, co-creation and practice improvement
abstract: In a time of interconnected social, political and environmental crises, international commitments to act on climate change and biodiversity loss are being put to the test. Upholding these commitments requires us to adopt monitoring and evaluation practices that bridge the gap between international ambitions and local action in cities. For safeguarding current progress and supporting urban nature, we argue that it is critical to reframe monitoring and evaluation as a collective learning process that recognizes people’s everyday knowledge and leverages community involvement to respond to changing conditions.

title: Residents near small rivers in the USA could face disproportionately high future flood risk
abstract: Analysis combining high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations and demographic projections across the contiguous USA suggests that residents near small rivers face a disproportionately higher flood risk by 2050 than those near larger ones. This enhanced flood risk is mainly due to low defence levels and increases in projected flood magnitude under climate change.

title: Evidence and limits of restitution
abstract: Assessing whether returning land to Indigenous communities delivers on its environmental promise requires evidence that goes beyond titling of continuously occupied lands. A study now uses three decades of satellite data on Mapuche land restitution in Chile to show how restitution reshapes landscapes, but opens space to ask what such evidence can and cannot see.

title: Environmental impacts of Indigenous land restitution in Chile
abstract: In an effort to redress historical dispossession and support Indigenous self-determination, multiple countries have adopted policies that return land to Indigenous peoples. Such land restitution programmes are partially motivated by a hope that restitution will enable Indigenous communities to influence land use in ways that will also generate public environmental benefits. However, little is known about how Indigenous communities change land use after land is returned to their stewardship. Here we show the land-use impacts of a Chilean restitution programme that, between 1994 and 2022, returned 217,716 ha of land to Mapuche communities. Using a difference-in-differences research design, we find that land restitution led to more grasslands, a common Mapuche use of land, and fewer non-native forest plantations, a use of land that the Mapuche have frequently protested against. However, restitution did not change the extent of natural forests. Given this reconfiguration of land use, restitution has led to insignificant changes in carbon sequestration or biodiversity. Our results complicate common narratives that Indigenous land reform will always yield improvements in environmental outcomes. Careful consideration of the local cultural context and the legacies of dispossession can help to set appropriate expectations for the environmental co-benefits of these reforms.

title: Author Correction: Spatial assessment of tap-water safety in China
Recognizing the human health impacts of marine heatwaves
abstract: Although the physical and ecological impacts of marine heatwaves are well recognized, their cascading consequences for human health remain poorly understood. We argue that marine heatwaves pose growing physical and mental health risks that must be treated as a distinct, core climate concern requiring anticipatory action.

title: African water research beyond the narratives of conflict and scarcity
abstract: Reproducible, replicable and robust African water research remains underrepresented in highly visible scientific journals, leading regional policymakers to turn to consulting firms and interest groups. We call for stronger editorial engagement with African water research to leverage its contributions to transboundary conflict resolution.

title: The true impacts of the built environment
abstract: Cement and concrete underpin modern societies, yet their true resource demands and the dynamics that govern their efficient use remain poorly understood. Two recent studies suggest that the most powerful levers for change may not lie inside the cement plant at all.

title: Culturalizing sustainability
abstract: Policy-makers and scientists dominate high-level sustainability debates but any decision that follows has consequences for ordinary people in their local communities and environments. We asked experts to reflect on the importance of embracing a culturally informed, bottom-up approach to the sustainability discourse and action.

title: Drought amplifies the psychological burden of war
abstract: The convergence of climate shocks and armed conflict poses a critical threat to human security and sustainable development. However, their joint impacts on human populations, particularly the erosion of psychosocial resilience, remain poorly quantified. Here, integrating georeferenced drought data from respondents’ pre-displacement regions with survey data from Syrian and Iraqi refugees ( N = 3,751), we find that the association between war exposure and post-traumatic stress is stronger among those from more drought-affected areas of origin. Under severe drought conditions, the increase in post-traumatic stress associated with war exposure was more than twice as large as under average moisture conditions. This pattern is consistent with resilience corrosion, whereby climate-induced hardship may degrade mental health and weaken the adaptive capacities communities need to navigate future shocks. These findings support policy approaches that integrate mental health into climate adaptation and humanitarian response in settings shaped by overlapping crises.

title: When drought meets war trauma
abstract: The human consequences of armed conflict and climate change are often studied separately despite frequent co-occurrence of those events in fragile regions. A study now reveals a compounding effect of drought on post-traumatic stress from war, underlining the need for mental health services as a component of adaptation and humanitarian responses.

title: The politics of measuring sustainability progress and citizen science
abstract: Developing indicators, and the methodologies behind them, should make space for participatory approaches if we are to shape interventions equitably and effectively, argues Dilek Fraisl.

title: Research priorities for addressing global absorbent hygiene product waste
abstract: A major, yet largely unrecognized, source of plastic waste is absorbent hygiene products, which include child diapers, adult incontinence products and period products. These products contain substantial amounts of plastic, are materially complex and are socially engrained in essential hygiene and healthcare practices. Here we analyse the research priorities to create sustainable systems for absorbent hygiene product provision. The analysis is global and interdisciplinary in scope, addressing nuances in high- and low-income settings, and bringing together behaviour, material, technology, policy and economic challenges. We identify important opportunities for scientists to help avert the unfolding absorbent hygiene product crisis.

title: On the relevance of post-growth in China
abstract: Post-growth refers to approaches prioritizing human well-being and ecological sustainability over gross domestic product expansion as a primary objective of economic policy. While it is widely discussed in the global north and generally targeted at high-income countries, its relevance to China remains underexplored and largely absent from academic discourse. This Perspective discusses China’s position in a possible global post-growth transition and explores convergence and difference between post-growth principles and development priorities in China. We consider how China’s concepts of ‘high-quality development’ and ‘ecological civilization’ could integrate post-growth principles, and vice versa. Understanding China’s context is crucial for a collaborative, effective approach to sustainability and global equity.

title: Towards safe and just planetary boundaries for novel entities
abstract: The Planetary Boundaries framework shows that humanity is veering outside the conditions that safeguard the continued health and well-being of society. Setting safe and just limits for novel entities, specifically anthropogenic chemicals and materials, has been difficult because of their sheer number and diverse characteristics, hampering effective management. To inspire future work, we present a conceptual framework comprising three interconnected pillars, considering both well-known novel entities and ‘unknown knowns and known unknowns’. This framework is intended to assess boundaries and chart transformation pathways towards societal systems that benefit from novel entities while minimizing pressures on ecosystems and human health.

title: Advancing sustainable aquaculture with a zero-valent copper filter system
abstract: Algal blooms, caused by excessive microalgae growth, threaten water quality, aquatic ecosystems and human health by releasing cyanotoxins and unpleasant odours. Conventional algae elimination methods, including the use of copper sulfate algaecides, are chemically intensive and environmentally unsustainable. This study introduces an innovative filtration system featuring a zero-valent copper microporous filter (CuMF), offering a sustainable solution for aquaculture systems susceptible to algal blooms and associated harmful by-products. The CuMF achieves 100% algae retention while maintaining an ultrahigh water permeability (11,700 l m −2 h −1 bar −1 ), markedly outperforming conventional polymeric filters. Furthermore, the CuMF facilitates spontaneous Cu(III) generation for selective oxidation of extracellular organic matter via interfacial electron transfer while preserving algal cells for resource recovery. In aquaculture systems impacted by harmful algal proliferation, this filtration system delivers long-term stability, high-concentration algal biomass recovery, and efficient removal of algal toxins, odorous compounds, micropollutants, antibiotic resistance genes, and viruses, enabling closed-loop water reuse. Techno-economic analysis and life-cycle assessment validate the feasibility of CuMF, with a 64.8% reduction in economic costs and a 77.5–97.2% decrease in environmental impacts across 21 categories, compared with using algaecides. These findings position the CuMF as an innovative and environmentally sustainable solution for mitigating algal blooms and advancing resource-efficient, circular aquaculture.

title: Spiralling frontier threats in Indigenous Amazonia
authors: Eliezer Augusto Litaiff de São Paulo Aguiar
abstract: Indigenous Lands are critical for protecting Indigenous Peoples and the Amazon. Yet, they are increasingly exposed to socio-environmental frontiers, bringing violence, illegal resource extraction and deforestation. Urgent action is required to prevent irreversible harm to both people and forests, particularly in Brazil’s Vale do Javari Indigenous Land.

title: From corporate net-zero pledges to credible climate action
abstract: Corporate net-zero pledges have proliferated, yet evidence increasingly suggests that most fall short of real-world impacts. This reflects not a lack of ambition but a lack of scientific foundations needed to ensure credibility and integrity in corporate climate action. This uncertainty underpins a trillion-dollar question: how capital and policy mechanisms can be directed towards actions that genuinely reduce emissions. A scientific infrastructure built around four interconnected research frontiers can close this gap, making corporate climate commitments credible, comparable and policy-relevant at scale. This could redirect trillions of dollars in investments towards genuine climate action.

title: Psychological barriers to improving carbon competence
abstract: To effectively contribute to the mitigation of climate change, individuals require accurate representations of the greenhouse gas emissions related to climate actions across life domains. Although this carbon competence is generally low, the related psychological barriers remain largely unexplored, and few attempts have been made to improve it. Here we investigate how heuristic and motivated reasoning processes relate to mitigation potential estimates and evaluate corrective interventions. Across three preregistered studies ( n total = 2,924) we show that low- to medium-impact actions are more frequently adopted than higher-impact actions, and that knowledge about the differential impact of climate actions is limited. Our data suggest that inaccuracies are driven by individuals consistently relying on the availability heuristic and motivated reasoning to form their judgements. To address this, we identify perceived behavioural costs and social prevalence as reasonable proxies of the actual impact of a broad range of climate actions. Leveraging this insight in two corrective boosting interventions and informing about the most impactful climate actions only partly improved impact estimates, with considerable variations across individuals. Accounting for heterogeneity through tailored interventions appears crucial to overcome pervasive psychological barriers to carbon competence on a large scale.

title: Subnational mechanisms undermine transnational anti-deforestation policies
abstract: Dry forests are disappearing due to agricultural expansion and logging, driven by consumption abroad. The European Union deforestation regulation, which will come into force at the end of 2026, targets this problem by requiring imports into the European Union to be produced in compliance with the forest protection laws of their countries of origin. We analysed the implementation of forest protection laws in the Chaco Province of Argentina between 2009 and 2024 using diverse information sources, including 15,042 georeferenced forest-use permits and 127,632 wood-transport guides issued to agricultural and wood producers. We uncover six mechanisms by which public and private actors relaxed the provincial forest zoning law to circumvent the minimum standards of the national Argentine Forest Protection law, thereby expanding the areas where wood or agricultural commodities could be produced in compliance with transnational anti-deforestation policies. To prevent these maladaptive responses from producing regions, importing countries should demand products that cause zero gross deforestation.

title: A global atlas of soil microbial genetic resources exposes protection shortfalls
abstract: Soil-borne microbiomes harbour vital genetic resources, encompassing gene richness and dissimilarity, an indicator of the degree of diversity and distinctiveness exhibited by the gene repertoire of the soil microbiome. These genetic resources underlie key microbial traits and enzyme profiles that support terrestrial ecosystem functioning, including nutrient cycling, plant productivity and soil health. Despite their importance, global patterns and protection status of such resources remain poorly resolved. Here we compile 1,609 soil metagenomes to map global patterns of microbial functional gene richness and dissimilarity. Hotspots of gene dissimilarity concentrate in tropical regions, whereas gene richness hotspots are more widely distributed. Areas combining both high richness and dissimilarity are rare, covering only 5.5% of the terrestrial surface of the Earth, while drylands emerge as prominent hotspots for microbial traits and enzyme profiles. Fewer than 25% of hotspots for soil microbial genetic resources fall within designated protected areas. Notably, the global patterns of soil microbial functional profiles are largely decoupled from those of bacterial and fungal taxonomic diversity, suggesting that taxon-based conservation policies may not adequately safeguard belowground genetic resources. Our work provides an actionable baseline to integrate soil microbial genetic resources into global biodiversity targets and protected-area planning.

title: Sulfur-mediated electrochemical copper recovery from wastewater with net electricity generation
abstract: The extensive mining and processing of copper (Cu) generate substantial amounts of wastewater containing Cu. The toxicity of these streams and the rapidly growing global demand for copper underscore the urgent need for reliable Cu recovery strategies. Conventional approaches suffer from low Cu extraction efficiency, poor selectivity and the formation of low-value Cu products. Here we describe a sulfur (S)-mediated electrochemical strategy for efficient Cu recovery from wastewater with the co-generation of electricity. Leveraging the reversible S → Cu 2 S conversion, the S electrode acts as a redox mediator, achieving high Cu extraction capacity, excellent Cu 2+ selectivity and robust reusability. By coupling with a sacrificial iron electrode, a two-chamber device enables continuous Cu extraction from wastewater while simultaneously producing electricity. The extracted Cu 2+ is subsequently recovered in a secondary deposition cell, yielding high-value metallic Cu. A flow-type cell demonstrates stable operation with real wastewater over ~250 h with a cumulative electricity output of 1.00 kWh m −2 and Cu recovery of 2.02 kg m −2 . Life cycle assessment and life cycle costing indicate favourable environmental and economic performance, thus highlighting the strong potential of the system for scalable deployment.

title: Copper recovery that powers itself
abstract: Removing toxic yet valuable copper from industrial wastewater usually consumes energy and leaves low-value sludge behind. Now, a sulfur electrode is shown to selectively pluck copper from real effluent and recover it for reuse, turning a costly cleanup into a source of high-purity metal.

title: Author Correction: Biodiversity recovery is slow following clear-cut harvest of boreal forests
Scalable ambient fabrication of single-junction and perovskite–silicon tandem solar cells
abstract: Transitioning high-efficiency perovskite solar cells from laboratory scale to industrial production requires scalable fabrication under ambient conditions without sacrificing performance or durability. Here we report ambient-air, blade-coated perovskite solar cells and modules that achieve power conversion efficiencies of 26.6% (26.5% certified) and 23.2%, respectively. These devices demonstrate exceptional stability, retaining 99.8% of their initial power conversion efficiency after 1,200 hours of continuous light soaking. This breakthrough is enabled by a hole-transporting co-polymer, PNCC, which synergistically integrates triarylamine and carbazole phosphonic acid units. Comprehensive spectroscopic, spectrometric and morphological analyses reveal the mechanisms underlying PNCC’s superior functionality. Furthermore, leveraging PNCC’s high conductivity and morphological uniformity, we demonstrate monolithic perovskite–silicon tandem cells with a certified efficiency of 33.0%. This work establishes a benchmark for ambient-processed, stable photovoltaics, providing a viable, scalable pathway towards sustainable solar energy harvesting.

title: Mapping hunting probability across the tropics in space and time
abstract: Hunting is a major driver of global species extinctions, yet the spatial footprint and temporal trends of this threat are lacking at the global scale, limiting our ability to achieve international policy targets. Here we present standardized global maps of hunting probability across the tropics, based on a machine-learning algorithm trained on 2,463 hunted and non-hunted tropical sites, spatially and temporally matched to ecological and socioeconomic predictors. We estimate that the spatial footprint of hunting extends across the entire pantropical zone, with distinct hotspots of high predicted hunting occurrence probability in the Indomalayan realm (for example, China, Sri Lanka, western India), the Brazilian Atlantic Forest and parts of West Africa. Refuges from hunting persist in remote areas of interior Borneo, Papua New Guinea, Central Africa and the western Amazon. Enhanced human accessibility has facilitated the geographic expansion of hunting from 2000 to 2015, most notably in regions historically considered undisturbed and remote such as the Amazon basin, and in areas already facing high pressure such as China and Indonesia. Spatiotemporal dynamics also varied among realms. Our standardized spatiotemporal assessment provides a blueprint to inform conservation, supporting targeted management actions and informed policy interventions to mitigate hunting impacts.

title: Phased fuel transition for low-carbon shipping
abstract: Along the Asia–Europe shipping corridor, biofuels offer the strongest near-term option, potentially cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 31–47%, while electrofuels become more competitive after 2040 under the International Maritime Organization Net-Zero Framework. Policymakers could therefore adopt a phased strategy that prioritizes biofuels now and prepares infrastructure for electrofuels after 2040, to avoid locking shipping into transitional fossil fuels.

title: Integrating shipping growth and ballast water management to assess invasive species risks
abstract: Maritime trade supports global economic development, but it also links distant marine ecosystems and can move organisms beyond their native ranges. A major pathway is ballast water, seawater carried by ships for stability and released during cargo operations. These discharges may contain viable organisms that can establish as non-indigenous species, with consequences for biodiversity, ecosystem services and coastal economies. International ballast water regulation has therefore required treatment systems that filter, disinfect or otherwise inactivate organisms before discharge. Yet the protection delivered by these systems may be challenged by future growth in shipping and by variation in treatment performance across vessel operations and environmental conditions. Here we assess whether ballast water management can keep pace with projected changes in maritime activity. We combine machine learning projections of shipping under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways with a global introduction-risk model that explicitly represents compliance and treatment efficacy. We show that, even with widespread ballast water treatment, projected shipping growth can substantially increase future introduction risk unless treatment systems achieve consistently high efficacy. Across Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, future risk ranges from 94% to 900% of the 2018 baseline, depending on shipping growth trajectories, ballast water management efficacy and compliance. These results indicate that technology adoption alone may be insufficient to counteract the ecological consequences of expanding maritime trade. More adaptive ballast water governance, improved compliance and sustained optimization of treatment performance will be needed to reduce future biological invasion risks in a rapidly intensifying global shipping system.

title: Phased fuel transitions for decarbonizing the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor
abstract: International shipping stands at a pivotal juncture in its decarbonization efforts, yet a comprehensive assessment of viable fuel transition pathways remains scarce. Here we develop a dynamic life cycle assessment framework integrated with system dynamics to evaluate 13 alternative marine fuels (for example, ammonia, methanol, hydrogen and soybean-based biodiesel) for the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor through 2050. The framework incorporates climate impacts, environmental sustainability, energy efficiency and economic feasibility. Under three scenarios (Business as Usual, Most Economical and Maximum Carbon Reduction), this study accounts for key dynamic parameters, including technology learning curves. Results indicate a phased transition: soybean-based biodiesel offers a near-term solution, while electrofuels dominate after 2040. The International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework progressively narrows regional cost–emission gaps, whereas the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation introduces a cost premium of up to 7.6%. These results indicate that policy design and regulatory stringency substantially shape fuel transition trajectories for maritime decarbonization.

title: Black carbon emissions and climate impacts of cost-saving Arctic transit shipping through 2050
abstract: As climate change accelerates, emerging Arctic routes offer economic gains by shortening voyages but pose climate risks through black carbon deposition on snow and ice. Here we assess Arctic transit shipping at the global scale. Among 295 port pairs with reduced distance, only 249 achieve positive net economic benefits when accounting for fuel, transit, insurance, capital costs and turnover profits. By 2050, Arctic transit shipping could generate up to US$2.3 billion annually. Black carbon emissions are expected to reach 2,200 tons, with a regional maximum temperature response of 2.0–2.9 mK per US$1 billion of economic benefit. Rising fuel prices are expected to increase the economic attractiveness of Arctic transit shipping. Faster energy transitions could enable earlier decoupling of economic benefits from climate impacts, whereas slower transitions may require adjustments such as transit fees and insurance premiums to limit climate risks.

title: Beyond the engine room
abstract: Technological progress can help address the environmental impacts of shipping, but implementing solutions remains slow and problematic. Understanding shipping as a complex physical, economic and governance system is the key to accelerating a sustainable transition.

title: Diversity of circular economies from Global South evidence
abstract: The circular economy (CE) is widely viewed as a key global lever for sustainable resource use. However, CE conceptualizations have focused mostly on high resource use in the Global North, largely neglecting the drivers, solutions and enablers of circularity in the socio-economic contexts of the Global South. Here, based on a systematic review of 183 peer-reviewed articles, we assess how CE manifests in the Global South. We find circular solutions to be considerably more bottom-up, centring around community-level and often informal practices rather than the top-down, policy and industrially driven activities that dominate the Global North-informed CE literature. CE motivations similarly differ, being primarily rooted in socio-economic needs and cultural practices rather than environmental concerns. Finally, CE enablers are often based on socially and technically adaptive approaches rather than technological innovation. These differences reveal that inclusive circular pathways for sustainable development depend strongly on context, suggesting the need for more flexible and empirically grounded CE concepts.

title: Contributions of traffic to daily PM2.5 exposure and links to cancer mortality
abstract: People with cancer may be susceptible to acute environmental stressors, including ambient fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ), but the contribution of traffic-related particles to short-term cancer mortality remains uncertain. We analysed daily cancer mortality records by cancer site from 2000 to 2019 across eight countries (Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, South Korea, Mexico, New Zealand and Thailand). A time-stratified case-crossover design was used to assess associations with all-source PM 2.5 and traffic-sourced PM 2.5 (TSPM 2.5 ). The analysis included 9,223,612 cancer deaths. Every 10 μg m −3 increase in the 2-day moving average of all-source PM 2.5 exposure (lag 0–1) was associated with a 0.77% increase in all-cancer mortality risk (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.64–0.89%). The corresponding increase in TSPM 2.5 was associated with a 3.87% increase (95% CI 3.28–4.47%). Although TSPM 2.5 represented only 14.72% of total PM 2.5 concentrations, it accounted for 73.55% of PM 2.5 -attributable cancer deaths during the study period, equivalent to 1.21% (95% CI 1.03–1.39%) of total cancer mortality. Effect modification by age, sex or socioeconomic status was not statistically significant. Reducing TSPM 2.5 exposure may help lower acute pollution-related mortality risks among people with cancer.

title: Lessons learned from European land subsidence
abstract: Land subsidence is a global threat. In Europe, it impacts tens of millions of people by increasing flood risk and damage to the built environment. Land subsidence is the result of a combination of natural and human-induced subsurface processes, and there is considerable potential to mitigate the human-induced drivers through policy and legislation. We show how Europe is approaching the issues of measuring and addressing subsidence at a continental scale. We look ahead to the challenges of climate change and the energy transition in the context of amplifying the impacts of land subsidence, providing lessons learned from the European approach.

title: Maximizing electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction to achieve closed-loop reactive capture
abstract: Extracting carbon dioxide from factory exhausts or the open air is expensive, largely because it takes so much energy to free the trapped gas from the capture solvent. What if one device could instead convert that captured carbon directly into fuels and chemicals, while refreshing the solvent so it could be used again? This emerging route could make carbon capture cheaper and cleaner—but only if we master a tangle of competing reactions. This Review shows that converting as much of the captured carbon as possible is key to closing the loop and describes how researchers are starting to get there.

title: The changing economics of public lands in the USA
abstract: For over a century, economic ideas have shaped US public land management. This culminated with ‘maximum sustainable yield’ (MSY) becoming a central decision-making framework. However, the passage of major environmental legislation—echoing an American preservationist tradition—spurred the US Forest Service and other public agencies to reconsider this narrow utilitarian approach, setting the stage for the adoption of a social-ecological systems framework emphasizing ecosystem services and resilience—benefits that are largely public goods—aimed at achieving sustainability. However, a reorientation of US management priorities now may be afoot, with renewed emphasis on extractive uses of public lands.

title: Daily exposure to fine particulate matter from traffic increases cancer mortality risk
abstract: Evidence from a multi-country analysis of 9.2 million cancer deaths suggests that traffic-sourced PM2.5 might contribute to the short-term PM2.5-related cancer mortality burden to a much greater extent than would be expected from its share of total PM2.5 concentration.

title: A membraneless electrochemical system for alcohol-laden wastewater upcycling
abstract: Resource recovery from wastewater is critical for advancing a sustainable water cycle and achieving a circular economy, particularly given the vast quantities of alcohol-laden industrial wastewater generated globally. However, current electrochemical upcycling approaches for such waste streams suffer from high costs, operational safety risks due to oxygen accumulation and limited stability, especially when using membrane-based systems that are prone to fouling in complex wastewater matrices. Here we present a membrane-free electrochemical system utilizing a CoNi–perovskite catalyst that selectively promotes alcohol dehydrogenation over the oxygen evolution reaction by balancing *OH and *OCH 3 adsorption, enabling efficient upcycling of methanol-rich wastewater into industrial-grade sodium formate and high-purity hydrogen while maintaining oxygen levels below explosive thresholds. When applied to real coal-derived methanol wastewater, the system achieves ~85% methanol-to-formate conversion efficiency, operates continuously for 2,000 hours and demonstrates robust scalability and economic viability. This integrated electrolysis-purification platform transforms wastewater treatment from a cost centre into a viable pathway for sustainable manufacturing and circular resource utilization.

title: Land-use optimization for food security, bioenergy and forest conservation in Indonesia
abstract: Indonesia’s energy and food security policy priorities include achieving a biodiesel fuel blending ratio of 50% (B50) and self-sufficiency in rice production through the development of nationally planned food estates. However, these initiatives pose substantial challenges, including the threats of mass deforestation, land conversion and emissions, as well as competition between food and energy crops. Here we assess the potential land-use and emissions implications of meeting Indonesia’s ambitious biodiesel targets and rice production goals. Using an improved high-resolution land cover map, multicriteria evaluation and production scenario modelling, we analyse the spatial trade-offs between forest conservation, food security and biofuel expansion. Our findings indicate that achieving the biodiesel B50 target by 2030 will require extensive land conversion, including 4.85–8.55 million hectares of land, while efforts to achieve rice self-sufficiency could convert up to 2.3 million hectares, with notable overlap between food and energy production zones. Associated emissions—360–3,753 MtCO 2 e for oil palm and 509–1,297 MtCO 2 e for rice—could surpass historic emissions events, undermining Indonesia’s climate commitments. This research underscores the need for more integrated land-use planning balancing economic development with environmental sustainability and calls for enhanced policy frameworks that mitigate trade-offs between food and energy production.

title: Seagrass fisheries expose the poverty dimensions of marine conservation
abstract: People living in poverty depend directly on local ecosystems for food and income, yet the coastal dimension of this poverty–environment nexus remains poorly understood. We examine seagrass-associated fishing and household poverty using household socio-economic data from 156 Indo-Pacific communities, linked to estimates of seagrass-proximate populations. Fishing households were consistently poorer than non-fishers, and seagrass-dependent households earned ~23% less than other fishers. Complete seagrass dependence was concentrated among lower-income households, with each additional purchasing-power-adjusted dollar per day associated with a 5.5% lower likelihood of exclusive seagrass dependence. Scaled across the Indo-Pacific, these patterns suggest at least 18 million people in poverty may use seagrass meadows while fishing, including 6.5 million who depend on seagrass as their only fishing habitat. These results make visible a population of millions that depend on seagrass, underscoring the need for management that identifies dependents, protects legitimate access and addresses land-based threats that undermine livelihood security.

title: Global analysis of nitrogen inputs from irrigation water to cropland
abstract: Irrigation unintentionally delivers reactive nitrogen to croplands via nitrate-rich water, yet this input is rarely quantified and remains largely absent from nitrogen budgets and fertilization policies. Here we compile over 1,300 field observations and upscale them using machine learning to quantify the nitrogen delivered through irrigation and map its contribution across irrigated croplands for 2010–2019. While the median input was 19 kg N ha −1 yr −1 , 10% of observations exceeded 100 kg N ha −1 yr −1 . Globally, we estimate that irrigation supplied 14 Tg N yr −1 , equivalent to 13% of synthetic fertilizers used on croplands. Important clusters appear in regions with intensive irrigation and high nitrogen inputs, indicating that irrigation represents a substantial but underused nitrogen source. Our findings expose an overlooked component of agricultural nitrogen budgets that can reduce fertilizer overuse, improve nitrogen-use efficiency and promote nitrogen circularity in irrigated croplands.

title: 3D-printed living materials for anammox–denitrification coupling in wastewater treatment
abstract: Wastewater treatment, especially nitrogen removal, is a major contributor to global energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, driving the need for more sustainable nitrogen removal technologies. However, the practical application of anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) systems is limited by persistent nitrate accumulation, as efficient cross-feeding between anammox bacteria and denitrifiers is hindered by metabolite diffusion and retention challenges. Here we present a strategy using 3D-bioprinted engineered living materials (ELMs) with spatial confinement to enhance the spatial proximity between core species and retain the metabolites, thereby promoting multifaceted cross-feeding between anammox bacteria and denitrifiers. A sodium alginate/cellulose bioink was designed to print anammox consortia into a defined microstructure with both biocompatibility and mechanical stability. The high cell density within the ELMs enhanced microbial interactions, and spatial confinement activated synergistic metabolic pathways and facilitated the exchange of extracellular polysaccharides, amino acids and cofactors between key microbial taxa. The ELMs achieved a 71.43% reduction in start-up time and enabled complete nitrogen removal (100%) without external organic carbon supplementation, which was validated with real wastewater. This work provides a viable approach for the rapid establishment and enhanced performance of anammox systems, contributing to sustainable and energy-efficient wastewater treatment.

title: Emissions and system-level decarbonization pathways for global petrochemical production
abstract: The petrochemical industry is responsible for 13% of global industrial and 3.5% of total greenhouse gas emissions, yet a globally consistent facility-level emissions inventory is lacking. Here we present a bottom-up assessment of historical, current and prospective emissions from 37,379 production facilities, covering 81 chemicals and 2,043 manufacturing processes. We estimate that petrochemical production emitted 2.0 ± 0.8 GtCO 2 e in 2023 and this could increase to 3.0 ± 1.2 GtCO 2 e by 2050 under a business-as-usual scenario. Emissions are highly concentrated, with 53% of 2023 emissions arising from 10% of facilities. Among primary chemicals, ethylene and ammonia were the largest emitters, at 290 ± 50 and 250 ± 50 MtCO 2 e, respectively, in 2023. Our scenario analysis indicates that decarbonization efforts should prioritize the highest-emitting facilities through efficiency improvements, alternative fuels and feedstocks, alongside broad demand reduction and power grid decarbonization. The analysis provides insights for industry, researchers and policymakers to target effective decarbonization in the petrochemical sector.

title: Higher odds of produced-water-like chemistry in groundwater vulnerable to shale gas spills
abstract: Unconventional oil and gas development (UOGD), the extraction of hydrocarbons from shale and other low-permeability formations through horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, has bolstered the USA’s domestic energy production and economy. These benefits have been accompanied by public concerns about the industry’s impacts on drinking-water resources, the environment and human health. Here we explore the association between observed groundwater chemistry and documented surface spills from UOGD in the northern Appalachian Basin. Using published data from over 16,000 groundwater samples and high-resolution, physically based groundwater flow and transport modelling, we find that areas with high hydrologic vulnerability to surface spills exhibit a threefold increase in the odds of detecting chemical signatures resembling produced water or deep formation brines in domestic well water, even when accounting for other factors that may explain such chemical imprints. Across our study region, we estimate that over 120,000 people served by domestic wells reside in locations where groundwater is vulnerable to contamination from UOGD activities.

title: Discovering catastrophic weather risks
abstract: Climate change is one of the greatest challenges to humanity’s future and worsening of extreme weather is at the leading edge of concerns. The most extreme weather events contribute disproportionately to risk amplification because they account for such a large share of total impacts, and can trigger cascading consequences. Yet our ability to pre-empt such events is limited. In this Perspective, we urge more targeted research combining the power of human imagination with improved understanding of what is possible across impact-relevant systems—including in extreme climate states—to help identify, and avoid, catastrophic consequences from climate change.

title: Minimizing climate change adaptation trade-offs in African rangelands
abstract: Climate change is intensifying precipitation variability in southern African rangelands, challenging existing systems of pastoral management. Simultaneously, developments in weather forecast accuracy and access may enable pastoralists to effectively adapt to these conditions. Here we use a spatial agent-based model to study the benefits of weather forecasting for adaptive rangeland management with and without concurrent risk-smoothing interventions that buffer livestock losses during poor rainfall years. Given empirical and projected conditions across seven southern African countries, we show that precipitation variability can reduce average economic well-being and worsen inequality among pastoralists; that, when paired with the adaptive use of weather forecasting, risk-smoothing interventions such as the provision of supplemental fodder can buffer these effects without overstocking; and that risk smoothing is critical for scaling adaptive management practices. Overall, we show how pairing forecasts and risk smoothing can reduce trade-offs inherent to each intervention alone, supporting climate change adaptation at scale.

title: Boosting water evaporation with clever surface design
abstract: Efficient evaporation is crucial for solar-powered water purification, resource recovery and energy utilization, yet boosting evaporation without using more energy remains challenging. Here, a smart surface on which water binds weakly, thereby enabling rapid solar evaporation, makes clean, sustainable water production more efficient.

title: Accelerating water desorption at heterostructure interfaces for high-rate solar evaporation
abstract: Solar-driven interfacial evaporation represents a sustainable and cost-effective pathway for water purification, yet how to accelerate the kinetics of water molecule desorption on the surface of photothermal materials remains a critical and largely overlooked bottleneck. Here we report a dual-phase photothermal heterostructure designed to accelerate desorption and substantially boost solar-to-vapour efficiency. By tailoring the coordination between surface Ga 3+ sites on eutectic gallium indium and oxygen-containing groups on graphene oxide, we construct a graphene oxide–Ga 2 O 3 interface that minimizes bonding with water molecules, thereby lowering the energy barrier for vapour escape. The resulting thin-film evaporator achieves an evaporation rate of 3.64 kg m −2 h −1 with 95.3% conversion efficiency under 1 sun irradiation. Optimizing the geometry to a high-aspect-ratio configuration further elevates performance to 7.54 kg m −2 h −1 at an efficiency of 96.2%. The system demonstrates exceptional long-term stability, maintaining stable operation over 30 days under indoor conditions and 60 days outdoors, while retaining robust self-cleaning properties and resilience in harsh environments. This work establishes surface desorption management through heterostructure engineering as a primary strategy for scalable, high-performance solar evaporation technologies with implications for green energy and global water security.

title: Sequential electronic reconstruction enables durable oxygen redox in water electrolysis
abstract: Electrocatalytic water oxidation is central to green hydrogen production, but its efficiency is constrained by rigid scaling relationships governing conventional metal catalysts. Activating lattice-oxygen redox breaks these barriers, yet it often destabilizes the material, causing rapid degradation under demanding electrolysis conditions. Here we report a sequential reconstruction activation paradigm that enables sustained oxygen redox through electronically ordered lattice restructuring. Under anodic polarization, initial Se leaching from a Cr 2 O 3 /NiSe 2 precursor broadens the \({e}_{{\rm{g}}}^{* }\) band and accelerates * OH deprotonation, strengthening metal–oxygen covalency. Subsequent Cr leaching selectively depletes Ni-co-ordinated oxygen, generating spatially confined oxygen non-bonding states. This sequential electronic reconstruction yields a modified NiOOH phase that promotes lattice-oxygen participation while suppressing destructive redox delocalization, thereby establishing a durable oxygen-redox window at high current densities. Consequently, the catalyst enables anion-exchange-membrane water electrolysis at 4.1 A cm −2 at 1.8 V in 1 M KOH at 80 °C and sustains stable operation for nearly 3,500 h under accelerated ageing at 60 °C. These findings establish sequential electronic reconstruction as a strategy to decouple oxygen-redox activity from lattice instability, providing a design framework for durable, high-rate catalysts for water electrolysis.

title: Urban energy and transport impacts of autonomous robotaxi deployment
abstract: Autonomous mobility is increasingly entering commercial urban transport services through robotaxi fleets, while its impacts on urban transport and energy sustainability remain uncertain. Here, using more than 4 million order records from human-driven taxis and robotaxis in Wuhan, we examine how fully driverless ride-hailing interacts with existing mobility systems and shapes operational energy demand. Robotaxi activity spatially overlaps with human-driven taxi demand, indicating potential competition within on-demand mobility markets. Compared with human-driven taxis, robotaxi trips exhibit lower station-to-station ratios within metro- and bus-station catchments (46.9% and 61.6%, respectively), suggesting a more complementary relationship to public transit. Robotaxi operations concentrate on less complex street networks, and incorporating network complexity into the demand model improves predictive performance. Under an upper-bound dispatch and ride-sharing optimization scenario, the required fleet size could be reduced by 62.5% and daily energy consumption by 44.8%. These empirical findings provide support for aligning robotaxi deployment with urban sustainability goals.

title: Far-right political support and clean technology adoption in Germany
abstract: The diffusion of clean technologies is critical for climate goals, yet political polarization influences adoption. Here we examine how ideology affects residential solar photovoltaic (PV) and electric vehicle (EV) uptake in Germany, drawing on responses from a three-wave individual-level survey, municipality-level observations of PV and EV registrations and election results. Supporters of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) show significantly lower willingness to adopt EVs and, to a lesser degree, PV systems compared with supporters of the pro-environmental Bündnis 90 / Die Grünen (GRÜNE) party. However, polarization is not static. The relative adoption gap between municipalities with strong AfD support and those with strong GRÜNE support declined from 76% to 31% for solar PV between 2000 and 2023, and from 84% to 60% for EVs between 2015 and 2019. Here, using an instrumental-variable strategy based on wolf attacks as a predictor of AfD vote share, we provide complementary evidence on the relationship between far-right voting and the adoption of clean technology. Counterfactual simulations indicate that, by 2023, solar PV diffusion could have been up to 1.3% higher and EV diffusion up to 2.9% higher in the absence of rising electoral support for the far right.

title: Asymmetric Mo–Ni atom pairs enable scalable water oxidation at industrial current densities
abstract: Accelerating the global transition to sustainable green hydrogen requires highly efficient and durable industrial water electrolysis. However, the anodic oxygen evolution reaction remains a critical bottleneck. Conventional nickel-based catalysts suffer from high overpotential or rapid degradation. Here we overcome this limitation by introducing asymmetric Mo–Ni atom pairs with a shortened interatomic distance of 2.85 Å. This unique structural configuration enables an oxide path mechanism with direct O–O coupling that bypasses traditional scaling relations. Consequently, the catalyst delivers exceptional durability for over 2,000 h at an industrially relevant current density of 3 A cm −2 . When integrated into a laboratory-scale anion-exchange membrane water electrolyser, the anode exhibits low cell voltages of 1.78–1.95 V at 2–3 A cm −2 , alongside more than 1,200 h of stable operation at 3 A cm −2 . To demonstrate commercial viability, we integrate the catalyst into a 71 cm 2 per cell anion-exchange membrane water electrolyser stack, achieving hydrogen production with >99% purity while slashing energy consumption and production costs by 10–17% compared with commercial benchmarks. We further establish a mass-production line for these oxygen evolution reaction electrodes, proving their scalable manufacturing viability and potential to drive cost-effective, zero-emission fuel production at an industrial scale.

title: An historic fishery collapse driven by socioeconomic and environmental factors
abstract: In the Late Middle Ages, the western Baltic herring fishery played a central role in Europe. Salted herring was the basis for welfare and political power. We make use of a 450-year time series of Baltic herring catches (1200–1650), to identify which factors drove the herring catch dynamics during different phases of our time series. By the year 1570, the fishery suddenly collapsed, causing large-scale dislocations in trade, with major social and political consequences. Using a recently established bioeconomic stock assessment method based on catch and price data, in tandem with a loop analysis, we find that a combination of climate change, overfishing and socioeconomic factors can explain the drastic collapse of the fishery. The results underline the need for interdisciplinary approaches, including social sciences, to understand the dynamics of fishery systems. This has relevance for fisheries management today, in the Baltic and elsewhere.

title: Restoration-driven positive and negative leakage in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Habitat restoration is a cornerstone of global climate and biodiversity policy, with over 350 million ha pledged for restoration by 2030, yet it remains unclear how restoration impacts ‘spill over’ beyond implementation areas. Restoration projects could lead to increased tree loss elsewhere (negative leakage; for example, when restoration replaces timber plantations and/or impacts landowner earnings) or reduced tree loss within project areas and surrounding landscapes (positive leakage; for example, if restoration meets timber or fuelwood resource needs or creates restoration-linked employment). Here we assembled a geospatial dataset of 129,982 restoration polygons (~6.8 million ha) across sub-Saharan Africa to evaluate changes in tree loss across space and time. Natural regeneration and active restoration reduced tree loss by up to 9.1 percentage points (pp) within restoration areas and 8.9 pp in 10 km buffers after 10 years, indicating positive leakage. By contrast, agroforestry increased tree loss by 7.9 pp within projects and 7.5 pp in surrounding landscapes. Leakage magnitude and direction varied across restoration approaches and countries (−7.8 pp to +7.1 pp), underscoring the need for context-specific strategies. Integrating leakage safeguards into restoration planning, carbon standards and incentive schemes is essential for securing landscape-scale climate and biodiversity-related benefits.

title: Navigating the land–energy nexus for carbon-neutral power systems in China
abstract: Land availability is becoming a critical constraint on power system decarbonization, yet its economic implications remain unclear. Here we couple gridded renewable capacity assessment with a spatially and temporally resolved power-system optimization model to examine how land availability shapes the transition towards carbon neutrality in China. Results show that land is a spatially heterogeneous production factor whose marginal system value varies substantially across locations. Shadow prices of grid-cell variable renewable energy capacity constraints reveal that high-value land is concentrated in demand-proximate regions of eastern and central China, where additional renewable siting can reduce reliance on costly transmission and remote deployment. Under stringent land-use restrictions, renewable deployment shifts towards resource-rich regions, increasing northwestern solar deployment by about 48% relative to the base scenario and raising inter-regional transmission requirements by ~20% in 2060. Although carbon neutrality remains technically feasible, restrictive land policies increase annual system cost in 2060 by up to ~300 billion yuan (~US$42 billion) or 4.1%; as electricity market reform deepens, such cost differences could become more visible in market-based price formation, depending on market design and cost-recovery mechanisms.

Highly efficient air purification by a charge-induced liquid-lined filter
abstract: Air purification systems often face a difficult trade-off: achieving high pollutant removal efficiency usually comes at the expense of filter lifetime, energy use or maintenance cost. Here we introduce a charge-induced liquid-lined filter that overcomes these constraints through a three-stage absorption mechanism: long-range electrostatic attraction, rapid interfacial capture and high-capacity bulk-phase absorption. The charge-induced liquid-lined filter achieves single-pass purification efficiency up to 99.6% at a face velocity of 1 m s −1 , with a refillable and dynamic liquid lining that prevents clogging and maintains high performance over 3,500 h of continuous operation. A full-scale air cleaner prototype incorporating the charge-induced liquid-lined filter enables a clean-air delivery rate of 377 m 3 h −1 . We further demonstrate its broad applicability by implementing filters across a range of real-world applications, from personal protective masks to air purification systems compatible with microgravity environments. These results demonstrate a scalable, durable and energy-efficient pathway to sustainable air purification.

title: Green synthesis of hydrogen and formaldehyde from methanol with enhanced quantum efficiency
abstract: Catalytic hydrogen production from methanol offers a promising green route for safe and convenient hydrogen storage and transport and on-demand generation but remains challenging. Here we report a modulated single-atom-based catalytic cluster, assisted by a photon–phonon co-driven strategy, capable of achieving efficient hydrogen production from methanol solution with co-generation of green formaldehyde. By stabilizing Pt single atoms on TiO 2 surface through Li-modulated microenvironments, the PtLi 2 cluster-immobilized TiO 2 catalyst achieves an exceptional hydrogen production rate of 4.36 mol g −1 h −1 at 150 °C, corresponding to an overall quantum yield as high as 184%. Furthermore, a 21.2 wt% concentrated formaldehyde solution is synthesized, offering a potential commercial product for medical use. Here Li serves five distinct functions: retarding charge recombination, facilitating electron transfer, weakening H adsorption, particularly maximizing the Pt 2+ dispersion rather than Pt 0 and stabilizing single-atom Pt species on the catalyst surface. The resulting system enables stable operation for at least 19 days with a high apparent turnover frequency, bringing this sustainable synthetic pathway closer to practical implementation.

title: Air filters with sustained breathability
abstract: Although essential to protect human health, air purification technologies suffer from clogging, short lifespans and repeated cartridge replacements. A wet-interface filter design now addresses these challenges, enabling efficient capture of airborne pollutants while prolonging filter service time.

title: Design principles for functional carbon materials derived from biomass conversion
abstract: Biomass-derived carbon materials are increasingly central to negative-emissions technologies, yet their functional performance under realistic operating conditions remains difficult to predict. This gap reflects a fundamental limitation in current design strategies, which rely predominantly on static, composition-based descriptors. Here we challenge this composition-driven paradigm and propose a shift towards a pathway-guided perspective in which functionality emerges from dynamic carbon framework evolution. By integrating conversion pathways with operating environments, we present a conceptual framework that unifies synthesis, structure and performance, offering design principles for biomass-derived carbon materials and elucidating the inherent trade-offs among reactivity, transport and stability.

title: Limited agricultural gains but high flood risk from global wetland reclamation
abstract: In recent decades, wetland reclamation for agricultural cultivation has remained as one solution to meet rising food demand; however, its agricultural benefits and broader sustainability implications are poorly understood. Here we identify wetland-reclaimed croplands (WRC) globally from 2000 to 2022 and assess their crop production performance and flood exposure risk. Results show that nearly half of WRC exhibited lower crop yields than existing croplands, especially when cultivated with upland crops. WRC contributed only 0.1% to total crop production, yet more than half faced severe flood hazards, with an average flood exposure probability 23 times higher than that of all croplands. Globally, 60% of WRC are subject to dual vulnerabilities of limited agricultural gains and high flood exposure, especially in food-importing or low-income countries. These findings reveal the unsustainability of wetland reclamation as an agricultural expansion strategy and underscore the pressing need to reconcile food security with wetland conservation.

title: Assessing green-growth and degrowth pathways through institutional regime feasibility
abstract: Whether climate change policy should pursue green growth, degrowth, post-growth or agrowth cannot be settled by gross domestic product trajectories. The decisive issue is where each pathway places its heaviest burdens: on technology, well-being generation, energy demand, institutional capacity or political credibility. We extend the Kaya identity by decomposing energy intensity into the well-being generated per unit of output and the energy required per unit of well-being. The split locates stylized burden positions; a subsequent regime-feasibility test asks which institutions can generate and sustain the required movements, who bears costs and risks, and whether commitments remain credible over time.

title: Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil
abstract: Deforestation is a major source of global greenhouse gas emissions, and continued forest loss risks pushing the Amazon from a carbon sink to a carbon source. While recent work shows that productivity-led structural transformation towards less land-intensive sectors can reduce deforestation, the labour market implications of such pathways remain poorly understood. Here we address this gap by developing a spatially and occupationally explicit agent-based labour market model informed by empirically observed job-transition networks to simulate the ability of workers to respond to labour demand shocks. Our analysis reveals significant skill and geographic mobility frictions that constrain workers’ ability to adapt to structural change. Applying the model to productivity-driven development scenarios, we find that pathways delivering the largest deforestation and emission reductions disproportionately benefit high-skill workers while increasing unemployment among agricultural and other low-skill workers. Mobility-enhancing labour market policies can mitigate these effects, highlighting the importance of understanding labour market dynamics for equitable and feasible deforestation-reducing development pathways.

title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
abstract: Climate change mitigation reshapes the distribution of economic assets in the low-carbon transition. Here we quantify climate-related assets for 169 countries across four dimensions: fossil fuel production, climate change damages, renewable energy potential and land carbon sequestration capacity. We combine integrated assessment models, climate projections, economic damage functions and biosphere datasets to assess asset changes under multiple mitigation scenarios. Geopolitical challenges and opportunities arise from climate change mitigation because losses and gains across energy and environmental assets are country-specific, which we further characterize through a broad clustering and a detailed pairwise similarity analysis. Our analysis suggests comparatively moderate impacts for the USA, the European Union and China, highlighting the challenge that the largest economic powers may not be those with the strongest asset-based interest for climate action. While our framework remains limited, our data provide input for integrating other ethical, governance and socioeconomic factors in future analyses of opportunities and challenges for ambitious climate change mitigation.

title: Artificial intelligence for life-cycle-aware sustainable materials discovery
abstract: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the discovery of new materials, offering a route towards sustainable development. Candidates are nevertheless evaluated almost exclusively on functional performance. Whether a material can be manufactured at scale, how it behaves once built into a real product, what burden its production places on the environment and what becomes of it at the end of its life are questions addressed only after the choice has been settled, when little can be altered. Bringing these considerations into the discovery process itself is achievable and would yield materials that are sustainable not by accident but by design.

title: Material circularity implications of battery degradation in shared electric mobility
abstract: The electrification of passenger transport is central to climate mitigation but increases demand for critical minerals. Shared electric mobility and circular strategies could ease this pressure, yet intensive use accelerates battery degradation and may alter their benefits. Here we integrate province-resolved fleet projections, degradation modelling and dynamic material flow analysis to assess battery material demand and circularity in China. We show that the material benefits of shared mobility depend on battery chemistry. For lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC811) batteries, it reduces cumulative lithium savings by 2060 from 5.3–8.1 Mt under static lifetime assumptions to 2.6–4.7 Mt. More durable lithium iron phosphate and lithium nickel cobalt aluminium oxide batteries preserve or amplify material savings. Our analysis reveals a temporal trade-off. Shared mobility accelerates battery retirement and boosts secondary material supply, while second-life battery use delays recycling, constrains secondary supply to vehicle manufacturing and increases near-term demand for primary resources. Accounting for battery degradation is therefore critical to aligning shared mobility, battery choice and circular strategies with transport decarbonization.

title: Small-molecule-bound biopolymer networks for sustainable multifunctional composites
abstract: Multicomponent biopolymer networks are promising platforms for developing sustainable materials. However, weak coupling across mismatched heterointerfaces of different biomaterials limits structural coherence, load transfer and functional integration. Here we establish a natural small-molecule-mediated non-covalent heterointerfacial reorganization strategy and validate it using a collagen– Ganoderma lucidum mycelium–plant-derived anthocyanin (CMpA) model system. By combining molecular simulations, interfacial spectroscopy, mesoscale structural analysis and mechanical modelling, we resolve a cross-scale pathway in which anthocyanin-associated non-covalent contacts at local heterointerfaces are translated into pore-wall consolidation, lamellar orientational coherence and continuous load transfer. This cross-scale structural integration yielded CMpA films with a tensile strength of 63.55 MPa, along with UV-shielding, antioxidant and antibacterial properties, reduced oxygen and water-vapour transmission, and pH-responsive freshness indication, making them promising candidates for active and intelligent packaging. More broadly, the work links small-molecule-mediated local interfacial chemistry with mesoscale anisotropic network formation and macroscopic functional integration, offering a design principle for sustainable biopolymer materials that require both mechanical coherence and multifunctionality.

title: Binding dissimilar biomaterials
abstract: Biopolymer composites offer a sustainable route to multifunctional materials, but integrating chemically distinct biopolymers remains challenging owing to mismatched interfacial interactions. Now, researchers report a small molecule strategy that modulates biomass networks, improving their structural integration and functionality.

A circular oligo(disulfide) anolyte enables practical aqueous redox flow batteries
abstract: Aqueous redox flow batteries are promising for large-scale grid energy storage, but their widespread implementation is hindered by the lack of anolyte materials that combine high capacity, environmental compatibility, recyclability, low cost and long-term stability. While organic anolyte molecules offer a potential sustainable solution, integrating these competing attributes within a single molecular platform remains challenging. Here we report a recyclable oligo(disulfide)-based anolyte in which robust sulfur–sulfur bonds serve as redox-active sites. The anolyte is synthesized by ring-opening polymerization of potassium-form endogenous thioctic acid, providing a scalable route to high-concentration redox-active species. Paired with a sulfonated cobalt phthalocyanine catalyst, this oligo(disulfide) anolyte delivers a capacity density of 128 Ah l −1 with a 95.5% material utilization rate at 50 mA cm −2 . Using a carbon-coated sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone) membrane with a sulfur–sulfur bond concentration of 0.25 M, the battery retains 98.1% of its capacity over 2,200 cycles while maintaining an energy efficiency of approximately 70% at 100 mA cm −2 . We further validate the scalability and closed-loop recyclability of this chemistry in a 63 Wh stack. Our findings establish oligo(disulfide)s as a robust, circular redox platform, providing a pathway towards more resource-efficient and sustainable grid-scale energy storage.

title: Efficient carbon dioxide separation with molecularly thin bilayer carbon membranes
abstract: As an energy-efficient and scalable alternative to conventional chemical absorption, membrane-based carbon capture requires materials that simultaneously combine molecular-level thinness, precise sub-nanometre porosity and exceptional mechanical robustness—a longstanding trilemma in separation science. Here we report graphene–amorphous carbon bilayer membranes that overcome these trade-offs by way of a graphene-guided polymer conversion approach. Leveraging a super-spreading effect, we coat graphene with a uniform, ultra-smooth, polymer-derived carbon layer as thin as 2 nm, achieving a high Young’s modulus of approximately 26.8 GPa. Controlled pyrolysis of the polymer precursor generates a carbon network featuring narrowly distributed, high-precision ultramicropores. The resulting graphene–amorphous carbon membranes exhibit sharp molecular sieving (selectivity of >60 for CO 2 /N 2 , >70 for H 2 /CO 2 and >70 for CO 2 /CH 4 ) alongside an exceptional CO 2 permeance of up to 5,000 gas permeation units that surpasses existing benchmarks. This combination of structural integrity and separation performance enables efficient carbon capture across varied flue gas, syngas and natural gas streams, establishing graphene–amorphous carbon membranes as a versatile, energy-efficient platform for sustainable molecular separations.

title: A thin carbon membrane to capture carbon
abstract: Anthropogenic emissions are rapidly increasing atmospheric CO2 levels, with severe consequences for the global climate. Researchers have developed a carbon membrane as thin as only two molecular layers that sieves and captures CO2 with very high flux and selectivity, holding promise for climate change mitigation technologies.

title: Recyclable flow battery chemistry
abstract: Turning water-based flow batteries into a truly sustainable technology hinges on recycling the organic molecules inside the battery. A redox-active organic molecule has now been developed that not only outperforms the industry-standard vanadium benchmark but also offers exceptional reusability.

title: Adapting to the risk of Atlantic circulation change
abstract: Weakening Atlantic circulation could shift temperatures and rainfall across continents, raise regional sea levels, disrupt food production and marine ecosystems, and erode the ocean carbon sink. Planning in the most exposed countries does not yet account for these risks; we propose five steps to close this blind spot.

title: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
abstract: Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.

title: The SDGs need a subjective well-being reality check
abstract: As United Nations Member States negotiate post-2030 development frameworks, an important empirical question is whether progress on the Sustainable Development Goals is also reflected in subjective well-being. Across 42 countries and more than 100 indicators per country, the indicators for Sustainable Development Goals correlate with life evaluations in levels, but show little consistent association with year-to-year changes in life evaluations. This divergence raises questions for post-2030 indicator design.

title: On living and feeling better
abstract: As the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) enter their final years, there is a desire to reflect on their societal impact. A study now compares changes in the SDG indicators with changes in how people feel about their lives and finds no detectable correlation between the two.

Far-right slows energy transition
abstract: Political identity is known to shape climate attitudes, but its effect on real-world adoption of clean technologies has been unclear. Now, data from Germany show that rising far-right support slows the uptake of rooftop solar and electric cars. However, these effects are not large enough to stall the transition.
